title: arrival-pattern-stabilization-playbook
body:
Purpose:
This playbook documents a repeatable approach for making throughput benchmarks robust to arrival-pattern noise and priming artifacts. Instead of ad-hoc long warmups, we define a small, automated decision procedure to decide when a run has reached steady state for our serving runtime and therefore is valid for reporting throughput numbers and percentiles.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to sequence-generation workloads (autoregressive decoding) and chat workloads with caching (KV cache) enabled.
- Assumes bench harness can drive parametric arrival patterns (Poisson, fixed interarrival, burst-window) and control client-side concurrency and pacing.
- Focus is on single-model, single-backend machine pools; cross-shard variability is out of scope for this doc.

Key definitions (for this playbook):
- Arrival pattern: timing distribution of request arrivals at the gateway (Poisson, fixed-rate, microburst, mixed).
- Priming period: the initial interval where the server state (GPU kernels, caches, memory) is stabilizing and whose measurements should not be used for steady-state metrics.
- Steady-state readiness (SSR): the point when throughput/latency measurements exhibit stationary statistics within configured tolerances.
- Occupancy: proportion of serving device compute capacity utilized (approx derived from tokens/s and model throughput profile).

Goals:
1) Minimize false positives (thinking the run is stable when it is not) and false negatives (discarding otherwise stable runs).
2) Keep experiment wall-clock time reasonable (ideally <= 30 minutes per config).
3) Make runs reproducible across days and hardware revisions.

Methodology overview (high level):
1. Choose arrival pattern(s) that reflect target production mix. We recommend: a) fixed-rate ramp, b) jittered Poisson, and c) mixed-mode with periodic microbursts.
2. Use a three-phase execution per experiment: PRIMING -> ADAPT (fast probe) -> MONITOR (steady-state detection window).
3. Apply statistical tests across sliding windows to detect stationarity (mean and variance stability) on throughput and p50/p95 latency.
4. If SSR not reached within max-time, mark run for manual review and collect additional traces.

Detailed execution steps:
Step 0: seed and environment control
- Pin the model version, runtime flags, and kernel catalog for the run. Track git sha and image tag.
- Reset device caches where possible between runs (driver-level, memory pools) and document when resets aren't possible.
- Use a fixed RNG seed for any workload sampling (token sequences) to reduce content variability.

Step 1: priming (duration heuristic)
- Start with a deterministic ramp: 0 -> target concurrency in 90s using linear steps every 5s. This reduces initial microbursts from test clients.
- Short priming window: run for at least 3 multiples of the model's cold-start median response time or a floor of 60s, whichever is larger.
- During priming, collect fine-grained samples (1s buckets) for token throughput, GPU util, and kernel churn.

Step 2: adapt/probe (quick probes to set pacing)
- Run three 30s probes at target arrival rate with 10s gaps. Compute mean and variance for throughput and p95 latency.
- If variance > 15% relative to mean on throughput, reduce client-side jitter and re-run probes (helps isolate client pacing issues).

Step 3: steady-state monitoring window
- Enter monitor phase for N minutes (default N=10). Use sliding windows W of 60s with step S=15s.
- For each window compute metrics: tokens/s, requests/s, p50, p95, p99 latencies, GPU util.
- SSR criteria: last 3 consecutive windows must satisfy both:
  * throughput mean drift < 3% between windows
  * p95 drift < 5% and p95 stddev across windows < 8%
  * GPU util change < 4% (if util is noisy, use moving-median)
- If criteria met, mark SSR timestamp and record steady-state metrics from the union of those windows.

Step 4: validation and repeatability check
- Repeat the entire PRIMING->MONITOR sequence 3 times (fresh process) and verify the steady-state metrics are within acceptable run-to-run variance (throughput stddev < 2.5% across replicates).
- If runs diverge, collect perf traces and compare kernel invocation patterns.

Load generator configuration examples (client-side recommended settings):
- Generic JSON snippets (put into bench-harness config):
{
  "arrival_pattern": "poisson",
  "lambda": 25.0,
  "client_jitter_ms": 8,
  "concurrency_target": 50,
  "ramp_seconds": 90
}

{
  "arrival_pattern": "mixed",
  "base_rate_rps": 30,
  "microburst": { "burst_rate_rps": 200, "burst_duration_s": 6, "burst_interval_s": 120 },
  "seed": 12345
}

Notes on pacing: do not use purely synchronous blocking clients for high-concurrency runs; prefer async clients with explicit pacing to avoid client-side head-of-line effects.

Metrics to collect (minimal):
- client: request start, request end, sequence length, tokens emitted, error code
- server: internal request processed timestamp, model kernel start/end, kv cache hit/miss, GPU util, memory high-water mark
- system: host CPU, net drops, NIC err counters

Statistical tests and rationale:
- We prefer simple, robust heuristics rather than complex time-series models for automation. Sliding-window drift tests (relative difference between consecutive window means) are robust and easy to reason about.
- For critical benchmarks (release or SLA verification), complement with KPSS stationarity test / AD Fuller to double-check.

Edge cases and mitigation:
- Long tail regrowth during monitor window: trigger an extended monitor (+5–10 minutes) and collect traces for the tail requests.
- Intermittent GC/defragmentation spikes: correlate server GC logs to latency spikes. If spike frequency correlates with our priming pattern, adjust ramp to be gentler.
- Cache priming non-determinism: for workloads that cache embeddings or KV, add an explicit cache-seed step that issues deterministic prefix requests until hit-rate stabilizes before measuring.

Reproducibility checklist (quick):
- [ ] Image tag recorded and immutable
- [ ] RNG seeds stored in run metadata
- [ ] Loadgen config attached to artifacts
- [ ] Device reset or note + baseline util recorded
- [ ] At least 3 replicates completed
- [ ] Raw 1s-bucket traces archived

Common pitfalls we've seen:
- Underestimating client jitter: client-side event loop granularity can add 5–20ms of unintended jitter. Always measure client-side interarrival histograms.
- Over-long priming that hides transient regressions: keep priming as short as safe and use monitors to catch regressions early.
- Relying only on p50: p95/p99 reveal saturation effects; use them.

Automation recipe (CI-friendly):
- Implement the three-phase runner as a self-contained job: bench-run --config X --seed Y --phases priming,probe,monitor --monitor-minutes 10 --replicates 3 --artifact-bucket gs://bench-artifacts/${build_sha}/
- If SSR not found in any replicate, job should fail-fast but upload logs for triage.

Quick starter commands (example):
- bench-harness run --cfg arrival_poisson_25.json --seed 12345 --replicates 3 --upload gs://bench-artifacts/arrival-2025-02/
- bench-harness analyze --input gs://bench-artifacts/arrival-2025-02/ --report-format json --ssr-window 60

Observability hooks to attach during runs:
- Enable kernel-level counters and GPU traces for one replicate per config.
- Tag traces with run id, replicate id, and SSR timestamp so posthoc analysis can align events.

When to escalate to manual triage:
- SSR repeatedly not achieved within max wall-time
- Run-to-run throughput variance > 5% despite identical configs
- p99 shows bimodal behavior or multimodal latency distributions

Appendix: example results template to record per run (CSV-friendly):
- run_id,replicate,arrival_pattern,target_rps,seed,ssr_timestamp,steady_tokens_per_s,steady_rps,p50_ms,p95_ms,p99_ms,gpu_util_mean,notes

Contact and ownership:
- Primary: Asha Patel (eng-serving-runtime)
- Performance triage rotation: Jonas Müller, Maya Gonzalez

This playbook should be reviewed after any major runtime kernel change, quantization pass, or scheduler rewrite. Keep run artifacts for at least 90 days to enable regression debugging.

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- Can we instrument a lightweight SSR signal inside the runtime that emits an explicit "ready" annotation once kernel warm paths have completed? (tracking: JIRA INF-7389)
- Explore whether TTL-based cache seeding (best-effort) reduces run-to-run variance for chat workloads.

End of document.
